summary: A horror of fear, rage, and isolation, in which a snowbound father's resentment and the hotel's ghosts turn him on the family he should protect.

need-to-breathe.why: No one struggles for breath; Jack dies of cold, not suffocation.

hungry.why: Hallorann shows Wendy a storeroom stocked for a winter, and Jack is locked in it, but hunger is never felt.

thirsty.why: Jack says he would give his soul for a glass of beer, a craving for drink rather than water, and Lloyd obliges.

sleepy.why: Jack wakes screaming from a dream of chopping Wendy and Danny to bits, and Danny's visions come in sleep and in trances.

nauseous.why: Jack recoils as the woman in Room 237 rots in his arms, a horror of disgust rather than nausea; no one retches.

dizzy.why: Danny goes rigid and glassy-eyed in his trances, and Wendy staggers between visions in the last act.

fatigued.why: Wendy drags the unconscious Jack to the storeroom, Hallorann battles snow to reach the hotel, and Jack limps exhausted through the maze until he freezes.

pain.why: Danny appears with bruises on his neck, Wendy breaks Jack's head and ankle with a bat on the stairs and cuts his hand with a knife, and Hallorann takes an axe to the chest.

disgusted.why: The beautiful woman in Room 237 becomes a laughing, rotting crone in Jack's arms, and Wendy meets a skeleton party and a river of blood from the elevator.

over-stimulated.why: Danny's shining floods him with visions of the murdered twins and the blood elevator until he screams, and Hallorann is struck down mid-drive by a vision of Room 237.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The hotel is snowed in for the winter, Hallorann fights a blizzard to arrive, and Jack, hunting Danny through the frozen maze, freezes to death.

afraid.why: Danny is terrified of Room 237 and the twins, Wendy of her husband, and the film's climax is Wendy and Danny fleeing an axe through the hotel and the maze.

anxious.why: Wendy worries about Jack's drinking, his temper, and the isolation, and Danny asks Hallorann whether there is something bad here before they even move in.

panic.why: Wendy backs up the stairs swinging a bat and sobbing, locks herself in the bathroom as the axe comes through the door, and Danny flees Jack into the maze.

sensory-pleasures.why: Jack savors his bourbon at the Gold Room bar and embraces the naked woman in Room 237 before she turns.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Jack claims to be writing a novel and admires the hotel's grandeur, but no one takes pleasure in art.

fun-excitement.why: Danny pedals his tricycle through the halls, he and Wendy explore the hedge maze as a game, and Jack bounces a tennis ball off the walls.

love-romantic.why: Jack and Wendy's marriage, already damaged by his drinking and the arm he broke, is what the hotel finishes off; the woman in 237 is a lure, not love.

love-family.why: Wendy fights with a bat and a knife to protect Danny, Danny's shining keeps warning his mother, and Jack's duty to his family curdles into the urge to correct them as Grady did.

grief.why: Grief is barely felt; Wendy weeps over what has become of Jack, and the murdered Grady twins are a past horror.

missing-someone.why: No one is missed; the family is together, and that is the problem.

aroused-sexually.why: Jack is drawn to the naked woman who steps from the bath in Room 237 and embraces her until she rots.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Danny and Hallorann share the shining and a quiet friendship over ice cream, and Jack confides in Lloyd the bartender as his best friend.

empathy.why: Hallorann in Florida feels Danny's terror from across the country, and Wendy reads her son's fear and bruises.

compassion.why: Hallorann flies from Florida and drives a Sno-Cat through a blizzard to reach the boy, and Wendy nurses Danny's bruises and gets him out.

grateful.why: No one has occasion to be grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Hallorann helps Danny because he must; no one takes pleasure in it.

trustful-distrustful.why: Wendy comes to see Jack as a danger, Jack accuses Wendy of plotting to leave, Danny hides what he sees, and the hotel lies to everyone.

depressed.why: Jack sits blocked at his typewriter saying he has done nothing, and Wendy, snowed in with a man she fears, has no one to call.

angry.why: Jack screams at Wendy for interrupting his work, blames her for everything, and finally hunts her with an axe.

jealous-friendship.why: There is no friendship rank at stake.

hatred.why: Jack tells Lloyd about the wife who sucks the life out of him, and the hotel's Grady urges him to see his wife and son as ongoing costs to be corrected.

contempt.why: Jack mocks Wendy's suggestion to leave as a demonstration of her bad judgment, and Grady sneers at Jack's failure to control his family.

resentment.why: Jack rails that Wendy has ruined his life and that he has a contract and responsibilities his family keeps him from.

proud.why: Jack insists on his duty to his employers and his novel, and Grady flatters him as the hotel's caretaker who has always been here.

amused.why: Jack's grin as he says Here's Johnny through the splintered door and his Three Little Pigs routine are jokes only he enjoys.

sense-of-belonging.why: The Gold Room's ghosts welcome Jack as one of their own, Grady tells him he has always been the caretaker, and the final photograph places him at the 1921 party.

lonely.why: Snowbound for months with the phones dead, Wendy has only Danny and Jack has only Lloyd and the ghosts.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Grady tells Jack his wife and son need correcting, and Wendy judges her husband by the bruises on Danny's neck.

embarrassed.why: Jack is caught out when Wendy finds a bruised Danny and later the pages of his manuscript.

shame.why: Jack swore off drink after dislocating Danny's shoulder in a rage, a shame he carries and Wendy raises.

guilt.why: Jack's guilt over hurting Danny five months earlier is what Lloyd's bar talk helps him bury.

sad.why: Wendy cries over Danny's bruises and over the husband she is losing, and Danny speaks sadly through Tony.

happy.why: The family's drive up and the first days of exploring the hotel are nearly cheerful, before the snow closes in.

joyful-euphoric.why: Jack whoops with glee as he chops through the door and tosses lines from the Johnny Carson show.

effort.why: Wendy hauls Jack's body to the pantry and heaves at the dead radio, Hallorann pushes through the blizzard, and Danny runs the maze in deep snow.

focused-in-flow.why: Jack types with fierce absorption for weeks, producing only all work and no play makes Jack a dull boy.

bored.why: Cabin fever is the subject: Jack bounces a ball and mutters at his typewriter, Danny rides the halls, and Wendy walks the empty hotel.

distracted.why: Jack explodes when Wendy breaks his concentration, and Danny is pulled from play by Tony's visions.

impatient.why: Jack snaps at any delay or interruption, but impatience is swallowed by rage.

curious.why: Danny is drawn to Room 237 despite Hallorann's warning, Jack goes in to investigate, and Wendy reads the manuscript to find out what Jack has been writing.

surprised.why: Wendy is stunned to find a manuscript of one sentence, Danny rounds a corner into the twins, and Jack finds the pantry door unlocked by Grady.

awe.why: Wendy and Danny gape at the hotel's scale on arrival, and the ghost world opens before Wendy at the end.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Wendy doubts Jack's claim that Danny bruised himself, Jack doubts the woman in 237 existed, and Hallorann doubts the hotel is as harmless as he says.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Jack tells Wendy he felt he had been here before, as if he knew what was around every corner.

confused.why: Wendy cannot make sense of what is happening to Jack or of the ghosts she sees, and Jack is baffled when Grady denies killing his family.

frustrated.why: Jack cannot write, the radio is dead and the Sno-Cat sabotaged, and Jack loses Danny's trail in the maze.

uncertain-certain.why: Wendy wavers between calling a doctor, leaving, and placating Jack until the manuscript decides her.

understanding.why: Wendy reads the pages and understands what Jack has become, and the mirror turns REDRUM into MURDER for her.

inspired.why: Danny thinks to walk backward in his own footprints to throw Jack off in the maze.

satisfied.why: Jack grins with satisfaction at his jokes and his axe, and Danny and Wendy escape, but satisfaction is not the film's note.

foreboding.why: Ullman's tale of Grady, Danny's visions, Hallorann's warning, and the hotel's history fill the characters with dread from the interview onward.

nostalgia.why: Jack sinks into the hotel's 1921 past, where he has always been the caretaker, and Grady's ballroom is a lost golden age.

anticipation-suspense.why: Danny dreads what Room 237 holds, Wendy waits for the axe blow at the bathroom door, and Jack waits in the maze.

hope.why: Wendy hopes the Sno-Cat and the radio will get them out, and Hallorann hopes to arrive in time.

schadenfreude.why: Jack enjoys Wendy's terror on the stairs and taunts her as he chops through the door.

elevation.why: Hallorann's selfless journey is the film's one good act, and it ends under an axe.

rage.why: Jack's rage builds from shouting to the axe, the bathroom door, and the chase through the snow.
